title: Personal protective equipment in Covid-19: Evidence-based quality and analysis of YouTube videos after one year of pandemic
screen_reason: Content analysis of 144 English-language YouTube videos on PPE donning and doffing, appraised by three physicians against CDC step-by-step recommendations. It reports a share of items judged inaccurate with an explicit denominator (90/144 = 62.5%) and a veracity-strict subcategory ('False or without any supporting data', 22 videos). The headline 62.5% is dominated by an incompleteness criterion and is therefore coded QUALITY under the governing rule, but the 'false or without any supporting data' subcount gives a genuine CONTENT prevalence row, so the paper is eligible.

estimates.country: Not stated (English-language videos, worldwide; searches run through a UK VPN proxy)
estimates.date: Videos published after 1 December 2019; video data recorded 25 February 2021
estimates.measure_type: % of eligible PPE donning/doffing YouTube videos containing claims that were false or without any supporting data
estimates.value_raw: False or without any supporting data: 22 (24.4) of the 90 inaccurate videos; 22 of 144 eligible videos
estimates.denominator: 144 English-language YouTube videos on PPE donning and doffing eligible after screening, drawn from the first 50 results for each of 40 keyword combinations (2,000 videos screened)
estimates.definition: Video assigned the inaccuracy category 'False or without any supporting data' by the reviewers applying the misinformation tool after evaluating the video against CDC donning/doffing step-by-step checklists
estimates.misinfo_def: No formal definition of misinformation; the misinformation tool asks whether "inaccuracies were present in reporting information", categorised non-exclusively as (1) Incomplete presentation of data; (2) Inconsistent with CDC recommendations; (3) Weak or inconsistent supporting data; (4) Misrepresentation of data; (5) False or without any supporting data
estimates.source_quote: Inaccuracy reasons or non-evidence-based claims Videos, n (%) Incomplete presentation of data 81 (90.0) Inconsistent with CDC recommendations 45 (50.0) Weak or inconsistent supporting data 42 (46.7) Misrepresentation of data 32 (35.6) False or without any supporting data 22 (24.4)
estimates.page_loc: Table 2 and Results, 'Misinformation tool results', p. 302-303
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two medical doctors, both staff of the Intermediate Care Covid-19 Unit at the University of Naples 'Federico II', independently assessed every video; a third medical doctor from the same unit adjudicated all disagreements until consensus was reached. The external benchmark is the CDC donning and doffing step-by-step checklists. No kappa or other reliability coefficient is reported, only the consensus procedure.
estimates.moderator_quote: After evaluating the content of the videos according to CDC recommendations, the investigators judged if inaccuracies were present in reporting information. The inaccuracies reasons were categorized according to the following non-exclusive groups, as previously done: (1) Incomplete presentation of data; (2) Inconsistent with CDC recommendations; (3) Weak or inconsistent supporting data; (4) Misrepresentation of data; (5) False or without any supporting data.
estimates.notes: 22/144 = 15.3%, an exact part/whole from verbatim counts (22 videos with this reason, 144 eligible videos) and therefore R8-compliant; the paper itself reports 24.4%, which is 22/90 over the inaccurate-videos subsample. I report the corpus-denominator version because that is the prevalence quantity; an adjudicator preferring the paper's own printed value should use 24.4% with a denominator of 90 inaccurate videos, which would then be within_misinfo_content=true. definition_variant=true: this is the veracity-strict subset of the 62.5% row below. The categories are non-exclusive, so these 22 videos overlap the other inaccuracy reasons. borderline=true because 'false or without any supporting data' merges outright falsehood with unsupported-but-not-necessarily-false claims.

estimates.country: Not stated (English-language videos, worldwide; searches run through a UK VPN proxy)
estimates.date: Videos published after 1 December 2019; video data recorded 25 February 2021
estimates.measure_type: % of eligible PPE donning/doffing YouTube videos judged to contain inaccuracies by the misinformation tool (any of five non-exclusive reasons, including incomplete presentation of data)
estimates.value_raw: 90 (62.5%) videos contained inaccuracies, of 144 eligible videos
estimates.denominator: 144 English-language YouTube videos on PPE donning and doffing eligible after screening 2,000 videos (first 50 results for each of 40 keyword combinations)
estimates.definition: Video flagged as inaccurate on at least one of five non-exclusive grounds: incomplete presentation of data, inconsistent with CDC recommendations, weak or inconsistent supporting data, misrepresentation of data, or false/without any supporting data
estimates.misinfo_def: No formal definition; operationalised as the presence of 'inaccuracies ... in reporting information' relative to the CDC donning/doffing checklists
estimates.source_quote: According to misinformation tool, 90 (62.5%) videos contained inaccuracies.
estimates.page_loc: Abstract; also Results 'Misinformation tool results' and Discussion ('we recorded inaccurate contents in 90 videos (62.5%)'), p. 300, 303
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two medical doctors independently coded every video against the CDC donning and doffing checklists, with a third doctor adjudicating disagreements to consensus. No reliability coefficient reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: According to misinformation tool, 90 videos were defined as inaccurate. Specifically, 90.0% (n = 81), 50.0% (n = 45), 46.7% (n = 42), 35.6% (n = 32) and 24.4% (n = 22) were inaccurate for incomplete presentation of data, for inconsistent with CDC recommendations, for weak or inconsistent supporting data, for misrepresentation of data and for false or without any supporting data, respectively.
estimates.notes: JUDGEMENT CALL for the adjudicator, and the main coding decision in this paper. The instrument is called a 'misinformation tool' and benchmarks against CDC guidance, which would ordinarily make it CONTENT (guideline concordance stated as accurate/inaccurate). But the dominant flag is COMPLETENESS: 81 of the 90 inaccurate videos (90.0%) were flagged for 'incomplete presentation of data', and the paper's own example is videos giving 'partial information on the step of washing hands'. A wholly accurate video that omits a CDC step therefore receives the label, which is exactly the condition under which the governing rule assigns QUALITY. Coded QUALITY with borderline=true; the veracity-strict subcategory is captured as a separate CONTENT row (22/144 = 15.3%). An adjudicator who treats CDC-guideline concordance as sufficient external ground truth would recode this row CONTENT with breadth='misleading'.

estimates.country: Not stated (English-language videos, worldwide; searches run through a UK VPN proxy)
estimates.date: Videos published after 1 December 2019; video data recorded 25 February 2021
estimates.measure_type: % of eligible PPE donning/doffing YouTube videos rated at least good quality on the Global Quality Score (4 or 5 of 5)
estimates.value_raw: 78 (54.2%) videos were evaluated at least as good quality (44 partially good, 30.6%, plus 34 excellent, 23.6%)
estimates.denominator: 144 English-language YouTube videos on PPE donning and doffing eligible after screening
estimates.definition: Global Quality Score of 4 (partially good) or 5 (excellent quality, excellent flow, completely accurate information, very useful) on the validated 5-point GQS
estimates.misinfo_def: Not applicable: the GQS rates quality, feasibility and clinical utility, not truth or falsity
estimates.source_quote: Furthermore, according to GQS, 78 (54.2%) videos were evaluated at least as good quality.
estimates.page_loc: Discussion, p. 303; full distribution in Table 3B and Abstract
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Global Quality Score (validated 5-point instrument, original English version) applied by the same two physician reviewers with third-reviewer adjudication; DISCERN Sections 1 and 3 were applied in parallel (median Section 1 scores 3 to 5, median Section 3 score 4).
estimates.moderator_quote: The GQS is a validated tool assessing the quality, the feasibility and the clinical utility of each video. [...] Five possible scores from 1 (poor quality, poor flow, most of information missing, not at all useful) to 5 (excellent quality, excellent flow, completely accurate information, very useful) were assigned.
estimates.notes: QUALITY row, kept but excluded from prevalence: GQS is explicitly named in the governing rule as a quality instrument. 44 + 34 = 78 and 78/144 = 54.2%, consistent with the printed value. The full GQS distribution is poor 12 (8.3%), partially poor 21 (14.6%), moderate 33 (22.9%), partially good 44 (30.6%), excellent 34 (23.6%).

missed_or_uncertain: (1) The other three inaccuracy subcategories in Table 2 could each be turned into corpus-denominator rows (incomplete presentation 81/144 = 56.3%; inconsistent with CDC recommendations 45/144 = 31.3%; weak or inconsistent supporting data 42/144 = 29.2%; misrepresentation of data 32/144 = 22.2%), but the categories are non-exclusive and overlapping, and R4 favours a small number of certain rows; 'misrepresentation of data' (22.2%) is the closest additional candidate to a veracity measure and an adjudicator may wish to add it. (2) The full GQS distribution and the poor-quality share (12 videos, 8.3%) are additional QUALITY figures not made into separate rows. (3) DISCERN medians (Section 1 range 3-5, Section 3 = 4) are scale MEANS/medians with no share of items above a threshold, so no row (explicitly excluded by the instructions). (4) Google Trends relative search frequencies (YouTube peak 69.5% in April 2020, Google 72.0%; ranges 2.4-21.6% and 3.2-22.6%) are normalised search-interest indices, not shares of anything with a denominator, and are not exposure measures. (5) Authoring-entity shares (36.8% public health institutions, 22.2% alternative medicine channels, 6.9% individuals) and target-audience shares (88.2% health care workers) describe the corpus, not misinformation. (6) Per-authoring-entity quality rates (e.g. 40.0% poor quality among videos by individuals, 28.3% excellent among public health institutions) are QUALITY subgroup breakdowns, not the headline, and are not extracted per the rule to keep the main figure rather than subgroups. (7) View and engagement medians cannot be combined with the misinformation flag, so no exposure-weighted estimate is possible.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis. YouTube queried with 40 keyword combinations (Supplementary Table 1) after clearing cache, logging out of all accounts and routing through a free UK VPN proxy to limit personalisation and geographic bias; the first 50 results per combination were screened (2,000 videos), and after excluding non-English, live-action, interviews, news reports, off-topic webinars/lectures, non-medical content, non-donning/doffing procedures, duplicates and anything published before 1 December 2019, 144 videos remained. Videographic variables recorded on 25 February 2021. Content assessed independently by two physicians from the same Covid-19 unit against CDC donning/doffing checklists, with a third physician adjudicating disagreements to consensus; instruments were the study's misinformation tool (five non-exclusive inaccuracy categories), DISCERN Sections 1 and 3, and the Global Quality Score. No inter-rater reliability coefficient is reported anywhere. Authors' stated limitations: reliance on YouTube's proprietary ranking, English-only inclusion, possible misses from the search terms, subjectivity of the quality appraisal, and platform volatility. The corpus is rank-truncated and topic-restricted, and 88.2% of the videos target health care workers rather than the general public.
